messages.subject: Annotations of reference alignment
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was wondering if there is a way to access the annotations DArT gives for the reference alignment? I have a set of outlier SNPs (from RDA and LFMM analyses) and want to find out which gene and function (in the LOCxxxx format) the corresponding outlier Allele ID is.

The format of the allele IDs (e.g. 82202452-33-A/G) from DArT does not corresponds to the names of the locus of the aligned reference genome of my samples (e.g. LOCxxxxx).

Best,

Cilla

messages.subject: convert dartr to vcf keeping invariant sites to calculate nucleotide diversity (pi)
messages.subject_clean: convert dartr to vcf keeping invariant sites to calculate nucleotide diversity (pi)
messages.body_plain:
Hello all! :)

I have a DArTseq dataset of sardines for which I'm trying to calculate nucleotide diversity (pi) using either pixy or vcftools, as they consider invariant sites in the calculation (the recommended procedure; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1755-0998.12635). However, I'm not being able to convert my dartr object to vcf including invariant sites in the dataset - apparently, only SNPs are exported. The only filters I apply to my dartr object are call rate, reproducibility and Hamming distance, in this order.

Does anyone know how to convert from dartr to vcf keeping invariant sites in the dataset so it is adequate for pi calculations?

I'm using dartR version 2.9.7 and R version 4.2.3 (but I've tried with different versions of R and dartR also using a genlight object, and with different filtering).

Kind regards,
Jéss

messages.subject: Re: Annotations of reference alignment
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cilla,

Could you please expand on how/where you got the names of the locus of the aligned reference genome of your samples (e.g. LOCxxxxx)?

One way to do it is that once you identify the SNPs, you are interested in, you "blast" (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) the Trimmed sequences of those SNPs. If you have DArT data and read it to dartR, you can find these trimmed sequences in the slot your_genlight$other$loc.metrics$TrimmedSequence.

Once you identified the location of the SNPs by blasting them, you can start looking for the genes, proteins, etc, involving those SNPs by searching them in the many biological databases out there. Please look at the following link for a list of these databases. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_biological_databases

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject: Problems with gl.filter.hamming
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Is someone else having problems recently with the gl.filter.hamming function?

I'm re-filtering a dataset of ~80,000 SNPs (dart data, imported as genlight using gl.read.dart). I started filtering by call.rate and reproducibility.
I used to run locally on my computer in Rstudio and it used to take around 2 days to run gl.filter.hamming in the same dataset. Now it is taking much longer, even using the Rstudio AI, and locally is not even running because o memory limits.

Does anyone have a suggestion on what can be happening?

Thank you!
Julia

messages.body_plain:
Dear Luis,

Hello. I have tried to look but I am wondering if there is also a code which I can use to calculate different genetic diversity indices (allelic richness, Ho, uHe, Shannon div index, polyLoc, monoLoc etc.) for each individual/genotype within a particular population? I mean functions such as gl.report.heterozygosity or gl.report.diversity supply us a value with respect to number of populations. How can I also use these functions to identify in what are the values of these parameters in every genotype?

Thank you.

Best regards
Swati

> library(dartR)
> # test dataset
> t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
> # separating populations and storing them in a list
> t1 <- seppop(t1)
> # using lapply to recalculate loc metrics in every population
> t1 <- lapply(t1,gl.recalc.metrics)
> # MAF
> t1$SEVERN_ABOVE$other$loc.metrics$maf
> # PIC
> t1$SEVERN_ABOVE$other$loc.metrics$AvgPIC
>
> 2. dartR is designed to analyse diploid data. A nice article describing software to analyse polyploid data is Meirmans, Patrick G., Shenglin Liu, and Peter H. van Tienderen. "The analysis of polyploid genetic data." Journal of Heredity 109.3 (2018): 283-296.

I've been analyzing a Rad-Seq pop gen dataset and I used gl.report.heterozygosity to get per population Ho/He/Fis values, but we'd also like to have either a p-value or confidence interval for those values. Is there a way to do this either with dartR or with another package?

Thank you.

-Kris

messages.subject: Re: P-values or CI's for Ho/He
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kris,

I'm working on that. Hopefully, on Monday, the functions gl.report.heterozigosity and gl.report.fstats will have:
- 4 different ways to calculate confidence intervals,
- plots with standard deviation or standard error or confidence intervals.
- plots could be bar plots with error bars or violin plots  combined with boxplots.
- Parallelized bootstrapping (in Windows and MacOS) will be used to calculate confidence intervals.

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of gl.diversity
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Did you find any answer to this question?

I'm using the q profile obtained by the function gl.report.diversity and I came with the same concern/question as all of you, I did check and compare a few measures of differentiation for beta diversity like Fst, Jost D, etc, but couldn't find any that actually match with the output of $two_H_beta so any help will be appreciated.

Best,

Rodrigo.

El jueves, 24 de septiembre de 2020 a las 5:12:41 UTC-7, mm.j...@gmail.com escribió:
> Dear All,
> I am looking for answers to the same question. I am wondering if there is any feedback todate.
>
> With regards,
> Gati
>
> On Tuesday, 10 September 2019 at 13:13:39 UTC+3 soraia.b...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > Thank you for developing what it's looking like a very comprehensive and integrative R package!
> > I have some questions regarding the interpretation of results from gl.diversity, which might just relate to my lack of understanding of the functions.
> >
> > I calculated alpha and beta diversity for q=0, q=1 and q=2, and I'm now trying to interpret the data based on what is described in Sherwin et al. 2017.
> > I understand that for within population diversity, i.e. alpha values, q=0 represents allelic richness index, q=1 Shannon information index and q=2 heterozygosity index, and that these indices are represented by H values. These H values can then be converted to a common scale of effective numbers, D.
> > For between population comparisons of diversity, i.e. beta values, q=0 represents number of allelic types not shared between pops, q=1 measures the chance of a type of individuals providing info on the sampling locality, and q=2 measured the chance of two random individuals from different localities having different allelic types.
> > Please correct any of these if I'm wrong.
> >
> > My question with beta diversity is that the supp material of Sherwin et al. 2017 provides many options to calculate each of these indices, and I'm not sure what the output from gl.diversity represents for each index. For example, Beta diversity for q=1 can represent the Mutual Information (I) or Shannon differentiation, but I'm not sure what is outputted. Do we get only calculations of H and D and we then need to calculate these measures a posteriori with a different function? Can we interpret H and D directly for both alpha and beta?
> >
> > Any guidance would be most welcome.
> >
> > Best,
> > Soraia

messages.subject: Re: HWE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rita,

Technically, from one point of view, testing for deviations from Hardy-Weinberg (HW) proportions is performed at the loci level. However, you could also say that when you estimate FIS (i.e. 1 - (Observed heterozygosity/ Expected heterozygosity under HW equilibrium) you are measuring how much a population is deviating from HW Equilibrium. You can do this by for example typing in the R console:

> res <- gl.report.heterozygosity(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>)

I recommend reading the following paper:

Waples, R. S. (2015). Testing for Hardy–Weinberg proportions: have we lost the plot?. Journal of heredity, 106(1), 1-19. Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/jhered/esu062

But maybe what you actually want is testing for HW deviations by loci within each population. In that case you can use, for example:

> library(dartR)
> res <- gl.report.hwe(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>, subset = "each")

You could also have a look to our function gl.diagnostics.hwe which provides you with more insights for HWE issues.

We also try to provide in the functions' documentation helpful information, and the relevant literature, to help dartR users to solve by themselves this type of questions.

You can access a function documentation by typing in the R console a question mark followed by the name of the function, for example:

>?gl.report.hwe

You can also have a look to our tutorials if you want to learn more about dartR:

dartR -- R Package for SNP analysis | Georges Lab (biomatix.org) <http://georges.biomatix.org/dartR>

Cheers,
Luis

I recommend using a "relatedness_factor" of 0.3. Run the code below so you can get a better idea about the values of relatedness used in this function.

Kinship estimates for pairs of individuals who share less alleles than the population average are negative, as described in the below article which is the reference mentioned in the function documentation.
Goudet, J., Kay, T., & Weir, B. S. (2018). How to estimate kinship. Molecular Ecology, 27(20), 4121-4135.

library(dartR)
# filtering on call rate
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>,threshold = 1)
# coverting to dartR object, so we can rbind individuals without messing with
# the slot ind.metrics
class(t1) <- "dartR"
# adding a replicate for testing
t1 <- rbind(t1[1,],t1)
# correcting for duplicated name
indNames(t1) <- c("replicate",indNames(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>))
#running grm
grm <- gl.grm(t1)
# Running netwrok with grm matrix
grm_plot <- gl.grm.network(grm,t1,relatedness_factor = 0.3)
# converting matrix to three columns
res_grm <- as.data.frame(as.table(grm_plot[[2]]))
# ordering from higher to lower relatedness
res_grm <- res_grm[order(res_grm$Freq,decreasing = T),]
#printing the top five pairs with higher relatedness
head(res_grm)

To identify clones, I recommend using the below code:

# Related installation instructions see:
#   https://github.com/timothyfrasier/related
library(related)
# estimating pairwise relatedness
platy_related <- gl2related(t1, save=FALSE)
res_coancestry <- coancestry(platy_related,wang=1)
# formatting of data
res_coancestry_2 <- res_coancestry$relatedness[,c(2,3,6)]
res_coancestry_3 <- cbind(res_coancestry_2$ind2.id <http://ind2.id>,res_coancestry_2$ind1.id <http://ind1.id>,res_coancestry_2$wang)
colnames(res_coancestry_3) <- colnames(res_coancestry_2)
res_coancestry_4 <- rbind(res_coancestry_2,res_coancestry_3)
res_coancestry_4$wang <- as.numeric(res_coancestry_4$wang)
res_coancestry_4 <- res_coancestry_4[order(res_coancestry_4$wang,decreasing = TRUE),]
head(res_coancestry_4,10)

Cheers,
Luis

Hi Kimani,

One way to do it is:

library(dartR)
obj <- gl.read.vcf("cassava.vcf")
pop_info <- read.table("pop5.txt", header = TRUE)
pop_info <- pop_info[match(obj$ind.names, pop_info$id),]
pop(obj) <- as.factor(pop_info$pop)

Another way to do it is in our tutorial in page 11. We encourage users to first try the resources mentioned at the top of the home page of this google groups forum before posting questions.

messages.subject: blast filtering
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was wondering whether if there is a way of filtering a gl object based on gl.blast.

I want to be 100% sure that the SNPs I have align to a reference genome (samples are from decades old museum material).

I've blasted the original gl object to my reference genome and have a df of SNPs that have been filtered with blast. How do I now filter my original gl SNP dartR object by this blast df?

Thanks!
James

messages.subject: Re: blast filtering
messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

One way to do it is by filtering on evalue or bitscore, see for example, the code below. You can get more information about these two values here:

https://www.metagenomics.wiki/tools/blast/evalue

library(dartR)
res <- gl.blast(x= platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>,
                ref_genome = "chr_20_mOrnAna1.pri.v4.fa")

res_2 <- gl.filter.locmetric(res,
                             metric = "evalue",
                             lower = min(res$other$loc.metrics$evalue,
                                         na.rm = TRUE),
                             upper = 1e-20)

Cheers,
Luis
